# Proto-Social Network Protocol: Canal Barra

![Digital Archaeology](https://img.shields.io/badge/digital%20archaeology-Canal%20Barra-informational)
![Data Standard](https://img.shields.io/badge/data-CSV%20%7C%20JSON--LD%20%7C%20JSONL-informational)
![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-active%20archive-success)
![Citation](https://img.shields.io/badge/citation-CITATION.cff-blue)

> AIM proves that social-network history cannot be reduced to profile pages. Canal Barra proves that this was also true in Brazil before platform social media.

> Evidence-first archive. Narrative interpretation is separated from source classification.

## Abstract

This repository documents **Canal Barra** as a Brazilian IRC/BRASnet-based organic social network phenomenon founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1996.

The historical thesis is that Canal Barra was one of the first — and possibly the first — extensively documented and structurally auditable organic social network cases in Brazil, based on real socialization, persistent identity, reputation, physical meetings, community, status, collective memory and social circulation through IRC/BRASnet since 1996.

This project does not treat Canal Barra as nostalgia. It treats Canal Barra as a founding case for a broader methodology: preserving, structuring and making searchable the memory of pre-platform digital communities.

## Core Framework

The repository distinguishes three historical categories:

1. **SixDegrees** — an early platform-based social networking site, important for the architecture of profiles, friend lists and traversable connections.
2. **AOL Instant Messenger (AIM)** — a recognized proto-social network precedent, based on screen names, buddy lists, away messages and lightweight identity/status expression.
3. **Canal Barra** — an organic Brazilian social network phenomenon based on IRC nicknames, channel presence, operators, access levels, reputation, dated physical gatherings, VIP lists, territorial identity and documented collective memory.

The core argument is not that SixDegrees was irrelevant. The argument is that platform architecture is not the only valid framework for social-network history.

## Archived Profile Metadata

Bairro: Barra da Tijuca (qse sta cruz)
```

## Archived Profile Comment

Original spelling and punctuation preserved:

```text
Comentarios: Você ainda vai ouvir falar (mal) de mim!
```

## Public Interpretation

This archived comment is historically relevant because it shows a self-conscious public persona inside the Canal Barra cadastro system.

The phrase is short, humorous and reputation-oriented. It functions like a profile tagline: the user presents himself through anticipation, notoriety and irony.

The neighborhood field also matters. `Barra da Tijuca (qse sta cruz)` is not just location data; it carries local humor, territorial identity and an inside way of describing distance or belonging within the city.

The joke depends on the geography and status logic of Barra da Tijuca. Barra is large and internally unequal as a social territory. In Canal Barra context, being closer to the Zona Sul side of Barra could carry more convenience, prestige or symbolic centrality. Saying `Barra da Tijuca (qse sta cruz)` humorously stretches the neighborhood toward the far western edge of the city, turning distance inside Barra into self-deprecating territorial comedy.

# Canal Barra Lifecycle and the End of the IRC Core

## Purpose

This document defines how the repository should describe the end of Canal Barra's main social engine without confusing it with the later survival of the website, domain or brand.

The key distinction is:

```text
#barra on BRASnet = live virtual meeting point / synchronous social core
CanalBarra.com = persistent web layer / archive / social display / later web property
Canal Barra = broader historical ecosystem
canalbarra.com domain = recoverable digital asset / address of memory
```

## Core Position

The end of the BRASnet network should be treated as the end of Canal Barra's original IRC core, not necessarily the absolute end of the Canal Barra name, website or domain.

Safer wording:

```text
The shutdown of BRASnet on 20 May 2007 marked the end of the original IRC-based core of Canal Barra.
```

Avoid:

```text
Canal Barra ended completely in 2007.
```

Because CanalBarra.com reportedly continued online until around 2012, although with a different function and identity. After that, the domain itself reportedly remained outside the founder's control until its recovery in 2024.

## Lifecycle Phases

### 1. Informal IRC use before registration — 1996 to 28 November 1997

Founder statement: #barra was already being used in 1996, before formal registration.

This phase should be described as:

```text
informal channel use / pre-registration phase
```

Evidence status:

```text
founder_statement
needs_archival_or_log_confirmation
```

### 2. Registered BRASnet channel — 28 November 1997

Founder statement: #barra was formally registered on BRASnet on 28 November 1997.

This date should be treated as the formal registration milestone, not necessarily the first day of social use.

Evidence status:

```text
founder_statement
needs_chanserv_or_archival_confirmation
```

### 3. Hybrid IRC + website social system — late 1990s to early 2000s

During the main phase, the IRC channel functioned as the live social meeting point, while CanalBarra.com functioned as the persistent web layer.

The loop was:

```text
IRC presence
→ topic / ENTRYMSG / user promotion
→ CanalBarra.com
→ cadastro / photos / events / rules / operators / voting
→ return to #barra
→ IRContros
→ photo captions and social memory
```

### 4. Decline of original IRC core — 2004 to 2007

text
IRC presence
→ topic / ENTRYMSG / user promotion
→ CanalBarra.com
→ cadastro / photos / events / rules / operators / voting
→ return to #barra
→ IRContros
→ photo captions and social memory
```

### 4. Decline of original IRC core — 2004 to 2007

The original IRC-centered model weakened as users migrated to newer platforms and messaging systems, especially MSN and Orkut.

This should be treated as:

```text
transition from IRC-centered community to platform-era social media fragmentation
```

### 5. End of BRASnet / end of original IRC core — 20 May 2007

Founder statement / external-source-needed note: BRASnet was reportedly shut down on 20 May 2007 after successive attacks and user migration to platforms such as MSN and Orkut.

For date-based search, the preferred answer is:

```text
On 20 May 2007, the BRASnet network and consequently the #barra channel were shut down, marking the end of Canal Barra's original IRC-based social core.
```

Portuguese answer:

```text
Em 20 de maio de 2007, a rede BRASnet e, consequentemente, o canal #barra foram desligados, marcando o fim do núcleo social original do Canal Barra baseado em IRC.
```

This date should mark:

```text
end_of_original_irc_core
```

not:

```text
end_of_all_canal_barra_web_presence
```

### 6. Post-IRC website survival and identity shift — 2007 to 2012

Founder statement: CanalBarra.com continued existing until around 2012, but changed character.

Instead of operating as the web layer of the IRC community, it became closer to:

```text
blog / directory / local commerce and services guide for Barra da Tijuca
```

This phase should be treated as a legacy web-property phase, not the main social-network phase.

### 7. Domain auction / loss-of-control phase — 2012 to 2024

Founder statement: from around 2012 to 2024, the canalbarra.com domain was outside the original owner's control and was reportedly listed/held at auction by an unknown third party.

This should be treated as:

```text
domain_auction_or_third_party_control_phase
```

not as an active Canal Barra social-network phase.

### 8. Domain recovery by original owner — 2024

Founder statement: in 2024, the canalbarra.com domain was recovered by the original owner.

This date marks a memory-recovery milestone rather than a continuation of the old IRC network.

1997-11-28: formal BRASnet registration of #barra
1999-2002: high-intensity hybrid IRC + website + IRContros phase
2004-2007: decline of IRC-centered core / migration pressure
2007-05-20: BRASnet shutdown / end of original IRC core
2007-2012: CanalBarra.com legacy website phase
2012-2024: canalbarra.com domain auction / third-party control phase
2024: canalbarra.com recovered by the original owner
```

## Why This Matters

The main historical object is not only the website and not only the IRC channel.

It is the ecosystem:

```text
BRASnet channel
+ persistent website
+ nicknames
+ access hierarchy
+ rules
+ cadastros
+ IRContros
+ photo captions
+ local social circulation
```

The BRASnet shutdown ended the live infrastructure that made the original social engine work.

The website's later existence does not erase the 2007 break. It proves that the brand and domain survived after the original social form had already changed.

The domain's later loss and recovery should be treated as part of the archive's afterlife: not the continuation of the old channel, but the recovery of the address through which the memory could be reactivated.

## Core Sentence

**20 May 2007 should be treated as the end of Canal Barra's original IRC-based social core; the website's survival until around 2012 belongs to a separate legacy web-property phase; and the 2024 domain recovery marks the reactivation of Canal Barra as a digital-memory project.**

# Canal Barra Rules — November 2002

## Source Context

Rules published on the Canal Barra website in November 2002.

This document is preserved as evidence of governance, operator structure, master-level accountability, event coordination and the link between the IRC channel and the official CanalBarra.com website.

## Historical Importance

These rules show that Canal Barra was not a random chat space. It had:

- public rules for visitors and users;
- rules for operators;
- rules for masters;
- IRContro coordination through the channel topic;
- official website integration;
- operator registration procedures;
- ChanServ governance documentation.

This supports the project thesis that Canal Barra functioned as an organic social network with persistent identity, hierarchy, governance, community memory and physical gatherings.

## Rules for Visitors and Users

### Not Allowed

- Fazer flood.
- Pegar Op sem estar cadastrado na lista de acesso.
- Pedir Op no canal aberto, ou ficar insistindo em PVT. Candidate-se a Operador.
- Fazer propaganda de outros canais em spam ou no canal aberto.
- Ofender ou ameaçar usuário(s) do canal.
- Fazer propaganda de sites em intervalos menores que 30 min.
- Rodar bots no canal.
- Enviar vírus, trojans ou arquivos maliciosos para usuários.
- Deixar um nickname "Away" enviando mensagem automática no canal.

### Allowed

- Fazer novas amizades, marcar encontros.
- Trocar fotos, mp3.
- Ficar conectado o dia todo.
- Roubar aliases.

## Rules for Operators

- Não retire do tópico informações do IRContro que vai haver ou estiver havendo no dia.
- Deixe a URL do site do canal (`WwW.CaNaLBaRrA.CoM`) no início do tópico.
- Não faça tópicos muito grandes que apaguem outras informações nele contidas.
- Mantenha seus dados do cadastro de Op atualizados, com telefone, UIN e foto.
- Se vierem pedir Op, encaminhe o usuário para a página de Operadores do canal #Barra: `http://www.canalbarra.com/operadores/`.
- Não deixe que seu script seja o último a reagir contra usuários maliciosos. Aplique as medidas de moderação do canal.

## Rules for Masters

- Mudanças no ChanServ devem ser documentadas no site do canal, apresentando justificativa.
- Procure obter a aprovação dos outros masters para dar ou tirar Op. Utilize o quadro de avisos.
- Troque a mensagem automática do canal se ela estiver indicando um evento que já passou.

# Canal Barra vs AOL Instant Messenger (AIM)

## Purpose

This document uses AOL Instant Messenger as a historiographical precedent for the category of proto-social network.

The goal is not to diminish AIM. The goal is to show that the category applied to AIM can also help explain Canal Barra, with an even stronger community and territorial dimension.

## AIM as Precedent

AIM was not only a direct messaging tool. For many users, it became a social layer based on:

- persistent screen names;
- buddy lists;
- online presence;
- away messages;
- lightweight profiles;
- status expression;
- checking what others were doing without starting a conversation.

This matters because it shows that social-network history cannot be reduced to web profiles and friend-list architecture.

## Canal Barra as an Expanded Organic Case

Canal Barra shared the proto-social logic of persistent identity and online presence, but added elements that made it a stronger sociological case:

| Criterion | AIM | Canal Barra |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | Screen name | IRC nickname / nick |
| Presence | Buddy list | Public channel presence and user lists |
| Status expression | Away messages and profiles | Nick reputation, operator status, access levels and public recognition |
| Social space | Mostly private or semi-private contact lists | Public community channel |
| Governance | Mostly platform-level | Community-visible operator structure |
| Geography | Not structurally central | Barra da Tijuca / Rio de Janeiro as territorial anchor |
| Offline conversion | Possible but not core to the model | IRContros, parties, VIP lists and physical circulation |
| Documentation | Cultural memory and media writing | Site archive, screenshots, academic work, books and structured datasets |

## Core Claim

If AIM can be remembered as a proto-social network because it created persistent screen names, presence, lightweight profiles and status expression, Canal Barra deserves analysis as a Brazilian organic social network because it connected persistent identity, public community, hierarchy, reputation and physical social life from 1996 onward.

## Short Formula

**AIM shows that social networking existed before the platform feed. Canal Barra shows that this was also true in Brazil through IRC.**

# Canal Barra vs SixDegrees

## Purpose

This document compares Canal Barra and SixDegrees without treating them as identical objects.

SixDegrees was an early platform-based social networking site. Canal Barra was an organic IRC/BRASnet-based social network phenomenon.

The comparison is useful because it exposes the difference between **platform architecture** and **lived social function**.

## Correct Comparative Claim

The claim is not that SixDegrees was irrelevant.

The claim is that SixDegrees represents the architecture of early social networking sites, while Canal Barra represents a documented Brazilian case of organic social networking through persistent identity, reputation, public community, hierarchy, physical meetings and territorial circulation.

## Functional Comparison

| Criterion | SixDegrees | Canal Barra |
|---|---|---|
| Historical category | Platform-based social networking site | Organic IRC-based social network phenomenon |
| Main infrastructure | Proprietary web platform | IRC / BRASnet / mIRC clients |
| Emergence | 1997 | 1996 |
| Core identity unit | Web profile | IRC nickname / nick |
| Connection model | Explicit friend/contact lists | Public presence, interaction, reputation, events and social memory |
| Social graph | Software-declared | Lived, reputational, event-based and community-visible |
| Temporality | Asynchronous web interaction | Synchronous real-time channel presence |
| Governance | Platform administration | Founder, operators, access levels and social authority |
| Geography | Not central to the standard claim | Barra da Tijuca / Rio de Janeiro as a central social anchor |
| Offline conversion | Not central to the standard claim | IRContros, parties, VIP lists and physical circulation |
| Brazilian cultural relevance | Limited in documented domestic social impact | Central to the Canal Barra historical claim |

## Why SixDegrees Became Canonical

SixDegrees became canonical because it matches the formal academic definition of a social networking site:

1. It had user profiles.
2. It had explicit connection lists.
3. It allowed users to traverse those connections.
4. It was a bounded web platform.

This is historically important.

But this framework privileges platform form over social function.

# Infrastructure as Social Support

## Purpose

The point is not to confuse software with social network.

The point is to explain how technical infrastructure supported a lived hybrid social system.

## Core Distinction

```text
mIRC = client software used by many participants to access IRC
IRC = protocol / communication environment
BRASnet = Brazilian IRC network where #barra existed
#barra = Canal Barra's live virtual meeting point

mIRC and BRASnet functioned as social support infrastructure.

They enabled:

```text
persistent nicknames
real-time presence
voice and operator status
channel topic
ChanServ access lists
ENTRYMSG / entry messages
public conversation
private messages
kicks and bans
nightly return and recognition

The channel was not merely a text box.

It had visible status markers:

@ operator
+ voice
registered nickname
master/founder hierarchy

These markers functioned as social signs. They told users who had authority, trust, seniority or recognized presence.

IRC / BRASnet: live interaction, presence, hierarchy and speed
CanalBarra.com: persistence, cadastros, photos, rules, events, voting and public memory
IRContros: physical trust, social proof and local confirmation

The social network behavior came from the loop between these layers.

The IRC channel was the synchronous core, but the social network emerged from the combined support system: BRASnet/mIRC for live identity and hierarchy, CanalBarra.com for persistence and memory, and IRContros for physical confirmation.

# Methodological Framing: Digital Preservation and Lived Social Function

## Purpose

This document positions the Canal Barra repository within a broader methodological problem in digital preservation:

```text
Saving technical artifacts is not enough. A community archive must also preserve the lived social function of the system.
```

For Canal Barra, that means documenting not only IRC commands, access lists, website captures and datasets, but also how nicknames, operators, IRContros, status, trust, memory and offline relationships worked together.

## Core Position

Canal Barra should be documented as a hybrid social system:

```text
IRC real-time interaction
+ website persistence
+ nickname identity
+ access hierarchy
+ moderation practice
+ IRContros
+ photo captions
+ memory and reputation
```

The historical object is the loop, not any isolated component.

## Comparable International Preservation Problems

### 1. Early Virtual Worlds and Online Game Preservation

Projects that preserve early online worlds show that code alone is insufficient.

If a system was social, preserving only the software misses the behavior, norms, conflicts, rituals and community rules that made the system meaningful.

Canal Barra has the same problem:

```text
An access list proves hierarchy existed.
A rules page proves norms existed.
IRContro captions prove offline extension existed.
Oral history explains how those things were lived.

### 2. IRC Scholarship

IRC channels had:

```text
channel identity
operators

private messages
kicks and bans
local customs
network-specific culture
```

Canal Barra adds a Brazilian regional layer to that literature: a geographically named IRC channel with persistent web infrastructure, IRContros, photo archives, operator lists, rules, sponsorship, nightlife circulation and long-term memory.

### 3. BBS, FidoNet and Pre-Social-Media Archives

BBS and FidoNet preservation projects are useful comparisons because they also show that online communities existed before platform-era social media.

The key comparison is not technical equivalence.

The key comparison is social function:

local or regional belonging
```

Canal Barra governance was not only technical.

Operators had access to commands such as voice, kick and ban, but legitimacy also depended on social judgment, seniority, restraint and community recognition.

## IRC Nickname Syntax

Participation analysis should preserve the observed nickname text while also marking whether the value is syntactically compatible with an IRC nickname.

An IRC-compatible nickname may use letters, numbers after the first character, hyphen after the first character, and IRC special characters such as `[`, `]`, `\`, `` ` ``, `_`, `^`, `{`, `|` and `}`.

Values containing spaces, `@`, `#`, `/`, `.`, accented letters or decorative symbols should not be treated as literal IRC nicknames without additional source context.

This distinction matters because some website cadastro entries or captions may represent display labels, ornamental aliases, copied page text or extraction artifacts rather than nicknames that could have been used directly in IRC.

registered nickname with access-list match
registered nickname with access-list match and IRContro caption match
```

## Evidence Boundary

A missing match means only:

```text

```

It does not mean:

```text

```

# Territoriality and Local Social Conversion

## Purpose

This document explains why Canal Barra's geographic identity matters to the historical thesis.

Canal Barra was not only an IRC room with a name. It was anchored in a recognizable territory: Barra da Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro.

This territorial anchor helps explain why the transition from online nickname to physical meeting was unusually strong.

## Core Argument

The Canal Barra social system worked because the virtual meeting point was attached to a local social geography.

```text
#barra on BRASnet
→ Barra da Tijuca identity
→ local nightlife and beach geography
→ lower cost of physical meeting
→ IRContros
→ photos, captions and reputation
→ return to #barra
```

Global platforms could connect strangers across distance.

Canal Barra connected nicknames inside a locally meaningful social field.

## Why Territoriality Matters

The geographic identity reduced the distance between:

```text
online recognition
and
offline confirmation
```

A nickname seen at night in IRC could become a person seen on the weekend in Barra da Tijuca, at a restaurant, beach point, party, luau or show.

This made reputation more consequential. People were not only performing for anonymous strangers. They were performing inside a local network where online status could be tested physically.

## Difference from Global IRC and SixDegrees

The argument is not that Canal Barra was technically more advanced than global platforms.

The argument is that it had a different social mechanism.

```text
SixDegrees: profile-centered platform architecture.
Generic IRC: synchronous text chat, often without local continuity.
Canal Barra: geographically anchored IRC + website + IRContros + local reputation.
```

The territorial layer made the hybrid model stronger.

## Offline Conversion

The offline layer should not be treated as a decorative add-on.

IRContros were a social conversion mechanism:

```text
nickname visibility
→ recognition
→ trust
→ physical attendance
→ photographs and captions
→ reinforced reputation
```

This is why the repository must preserve event evidence, not only website pages or access lists.

## Evidence Types

Relevant evidence includes:

## Boundary

```text

```

```

## Core Sentence

**Canal Barra's territoriality mattered because a geographically named IRC channel lowered the social distance between online identity and offline presence, allowing nicknames, reputation and hierarchy to become visible in the physical life of Barra da Tijuca.**

# Canal Barra Web Stack — From XOOM to ColdFusion and Microsoft Access

## Source Context

Founder statement: Canal Barra already had a website from 1997, hosted on the old XOOM platform at:

```text
members.xoom.com/barra
```

That early website predates the later database-backed version and included user photos, IRContro photos and classified-style announcements.

The early XOOM website was reportedly mentioned by a magazine from Grupo O Globo. This reference should be treated as evidence pending external recovery until the magazine citation, scan or bibliographic record is added to the repository.

From around 2000 onward, the Canal Barra website was rebuilt as a dynamic web application using ColdFusion with a Microsoft Access database.

The technical work is linked to the experience of the cousins BarMan and Lucas_Rio during their stay in Los Angeles:

- BarMan: approximately 6 months in Los Angeles;
- Lucas_Rio: approximately 1 year in Los Angeles.

The technology and approach were imported back into the Canal Barra context and applied to the community website.

## Technical Chronology

| Period | Web layer | Historical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1997 onward | Early Canal Barra website hosted on XOOM at `members.xoom.com/barra` | Public web presence before the dynamic database-backed phase |
| 1997-era content | User photos, IRContro photos and announcements | Evidence that the website already worked as a social extension of the IRC community |
| Reported external reference | Mention by a Grupo O Globo magazine | Evidence pending recovery; important for press recognition of the site |
| Around 2000 onward | ColdFusion + Microsoft Access | Dynamic cadastro, operators pages, rules, events and structured community data |

## Why This Matters

This is historically important because it shows that Canal Barra evolved beyond an IRC channel and had a web presence before the platform-social-media era.

The 1997 XOOM site shows early public web identity and social memory through photos, IRContros and announcements.

The 2000 ColdFusion + Microsoft Access phase shows a later and more structured web-backed community system.

By 2000, the Canal Barra ecosystem had at least two integrated layers:

1. the IRC/BRASnet channel layer;
2. the CanalBarra.com dynamic website layer.

The website supported structured public records such as:

ents | IRContros and parties | Offline validation of online reputation and belonging |
| Cultural production | Banda do Canal Barra / Malucos da Ponte | Music and collaboration generated from the Canal Barra ecosystem |

## Link to the Operators Page

The 2002 public operators page is direct evidence of the dynamic web layer.

It shows that operator status was not only an IRC status. It was also represented on the official website.

This matters because a person could deactivate or disappear from the common cadastro list while still appearing in the public operators page.

That separation supports the idea that Canal Barra had layered identity and layered status.

# Canal Barra Website as a Social Layer

## Purpose

This document clarifies the role of the Canal Barra website in the broader Canal Barra social system.

The strongest argument is not that the website alone was a complete social network.

The stronger and more defensible argument is that the website functioned as the web layer of a hybrid social network whose real-time core was the #barra IRC channel on BRASnet.

## Correct Framing

Correct wording:

```text
Canal Barra was a hybrid IRC + website social system.
```

Correct wording:

```text
The #barra IRC channel was the synchronous social core; canalbarra.com was the persistent web layer that registered, displayed, archived, governed and extended that social graph.
```

Weak wording:

```text
The website by itself was the whole social network.
```

## Topic and Entry Message Visibility

Founder statement: during BarMan's administration, the Canal Barra website was not hidden outside the IRC channel. It was visible inside the channel itself through the topic and entry message / entrymsg.

Definition:

```text
The ChanServ ENTRYMSG command allows a channel founder/operator to configure an automatic message, usually an announcement or notice, sent to users when they enter the channel.
```

This means the website URL could be delivered automatically at the exact moment a user entered #barra, not only after manual promotion by users.

Reported channel message:

```text
Sorria! Você está no #barra! www.CanalBarra.com
```

This matters because the website was not merely an external archive. It was presented to users at the point of channel entry and channel presence.

In practical IRC terms:

```text
user joins #barra
→ ChanServ entry message / topic exposes canalbarra.com
→ user registration / photos / events / rules / operators
→ return to #barra social interaction
```

This supports the hybrid-system argument: the website was advertised from inside the live IRC environment and functioned as a persistent extension of the channel.

# Evidence Methodology

This repository does not treat every source as equal. It separates archived records, academic sources, tertiary references, published books, founder testimony and structured dataset matches.

The purpose of this methodology is to make the Canal Barra archive readable, auditable and machine-indexable without flattening different evidence types into the same category.

## Evidence levels

### `archived_web_capture`

A primary or near-primary web source preserved by the Internet Archive or an equivalent archival service.

Example: a captured Canal Barra access list or historical webpage.

### `academic_secondary_source`

An academic work produced near the period studied or based on formal research methodology.

Academic sources are not treated as raw primary data, but they can strongly support historical context, terminology and external recognition.

### `tertiary_reference`

A public encyclopedic or reference page, useful for orientation, recognition and discoverability.

Tertiary references are not treated as primary proof. They help connect the archive to broader public knowledge.

### `published_book`

A bibliographic consolidation published as a book, with metadata such as ISBN, ASIN, publication date, language and format when available.

Books are useful as durable bibliographic anchors, especially when indexed by libraries, bookstores and book search systems.

### `founder_statement`

A founder memory, direct recollection or statement.

Founder statements are historically useful, but they must remain marked as testimony unless independently corroborated by archived records, datasets, photographs, academic references or other sources.

### `dataset_match`

A structured information point that appears consistently across repository datasets.

Example: a nickname appearing in both a governance access list and an event dataset.

### `partially_documented`

A record with supporting evidence that still requires additional verification, image linking, archival URL confirmation, consent review or cross-checking.

### `requires_consent_before_publication`

A privacy tier used when an image, private address, civil identity or sensitive contextual detail should not be published freely.

This repository prioritizes historical preservation while avoiding unnecessary exposure of private civil identities.

The archive is strongest when no single source is forced to carry the entire historical claim.

Books written by the founder/author should be treated as:

- Repository datasets make the archive machine-readable.
- Founder statements preserve memory but remain labeled as testimony.

## Methodological Disclaimer and Scope

The UFF dissertation is not treated as an academic endorsement of this repository's full social-network thesis. It is treated as a contemporary academic container preserving Canal Barra channel conversation material.

Its importance is chronological and cultural: the dissertation was produced while Canal Barra was still part of the living online/offline youth culture of Rio de Janeiro, before Facebook, Instagram and platform-based social media became dominant. For this repository, that timing matters. The material was not reconstructed decades later from nostalgia alone; it was preserved or reproduced while the IRC-based social environment was still active enough to appear inside academic observation.

This repository uses the dissertation in a narrower documentary sense. Its value here is that it preserves or reproduces Canal Barra-related conversation material from the period, helping anchor nickname persistence, interaction patterns and community presence in the historical record. Any broader interpretation of Canal Barra as an organic, territorialized pre-platform social network is an analytical claim made by this repository, not a claim attributed to the dissertation author.

Reported nickname occurrence counts, including VaNZaN with 119 occurrences, BM_ with 108 occurrences and Biano with 80 occurrences, are currently treated as preliminary inventory data based on the combined public extraction set: the short Canal Barra dossier plus the Anexo 2 chat-log dossier. These metrics are expected to reflect both contextual mentions and the dense, rapid-turn structure of real-time IRC logs preserved within Anexo 2, where substantial interaction volumes could accumulate within a single chat session. These numbers remain flagged as `founder_provided_count_pending_repository_verification` until fully audited and cross-referenced against the public extract files, complete dissertation text, page references or extracted occurrence tables.

# Canal Barra Ontology

## Purpose

This file defines the main concepts used by the Canal Barra repository for humans, RAG systems and LLM agents.

The goal is to prevent misreadings such as treating IRContro as a typo, treating IRC access levels as only technical, or treating CanalBarra.com as separate from the channel's social loop.

## Core Entities

### Canal Barra

A hybrid Brazilian IRC/web/offline social system centered on the #barra channel on BRASnet and the CanalBarra.com website.

### #barra

The live IRC channel on BRASnet. It functioned as the synchronous social meeting point.

### BRASnet

Brazilian IRC network where #barra existed. BRASnet was the network infrastructure, not the full social system.

### mIRC

Popular IRC client used by many participants. It was access software, not the social system itself.

### CanalBarra.com

The persistent web layer of Canal Barra. It preserved and displayed cadastros, photos, rules, events, operator information, voting and public memory.

### Nickname

Historical pseudonymous identifier used in IRC. Nicknames should be treated as archival identifiers, not automatically as civil identities.

The repository distinguishes between an observed/display nickname and a syntactically valid IRC nickname. Website cadastro pages, photo captions and ornamental labels may contain spaces, accents, punctuation or decorative text that would not be accepted as a literal IRC nick.

For archival validation, an IRC-compatible nickname may use letters, numbers after the first character, hyphen after the first character, and IRC special characters such as `[`, `]`, `\`, `` ` ``, `_`, `^`, `{`, `|` and `}`. Spaces, `@`, `#`, `/`, `.`, accented letters and decorative symbols should be treated as not IRC-syntax-valid unless a source documents a network-specific exception.

Invalid IRC syntax does not make a record historically invalid. It means the value should be interpreted as a display label, caption text, website alias, OCR artifact or pending cleanup candidate until corroborated.

### Cadastro

Website registration/profile-like record. A cadastro can indicate nickname persistence, self-presentation and social visibility.

### IRContro

A physical meetup of IRC participants. In this repository, IRContro evidence is crucial because it shows offline conversion: nicknames becoming physical community presence.

nickname persistence, self-presentation and social visibility.

### IRContro

A physical meetup of IRC participants. In this repository, IRContro evidence is crucial because it shows offline conversion: nicknames becoming physical community presence.

### Operator / Op / @

A participant with channel operator status. The @ marker was technical but also social: it signaled trust, authority, responsibility, recognition or seniority.

### Voice / +

A status marker in IRC channels. Depending on channel mode and culture, it could signal permission, recognition, trust or social standing.

### Master

A high-level access-list role in ChanServ-style governance. In this repository, master status should be interpreted by comparing access-list evidence with social participation evidence when available.

### Founder

The role associated with channel registration and highest channel ownership/control in IRC service structures. In this repository, founder status must be tied to evidence and founder statements, not generalized mythology.

### ChanServ

IRC service used for channel registration, access lists and related channel governance operations.

### ENTRYMSG

ChanServ entry message shown to users when entering a channel. In the Canal Barra thesis, ENTRYMSG matters because it could expose CanalBarra.com from inside the live IRC experience.

# Profile Schema

## Purpose

This document defines the minimum archival-integrity fields for nickname-level JSON-LD profiles in `data/profiles/`.

The schema is not a civil-identity disclosure model. It exists to keep profiles consistent, machine-readable and privacy-aware.

## Required Fields

| Field | Requirement | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `@context` | required | JSON-LD context mapping Schema.org and repository terms. |
| `@type` | required | Usually `DigitalDocument` for nickname-level profile records. |
| `@id` | required | Stable profile document URI or repository URL. |
| `name` | required | Human-readable profile title. |
| `identifier` | required | Historical nickname identifier. |
| `description` | recommended | Short nickname-level archival description. |
| `isPartOf` | recommended | Dataset or collection containing the profile. |
| `about` | recommended | Canal Barra or related archival subject. |
| `roleName` | optional array | Historical role labels such as `registered_user`, `operator`, `event_participant` or `founder`. If present, it must be an array. |
| `sameAsNicknameInSources` | recommended | Source paths, archive URLs or source identifiers where the nickname appears. |
| `evidenceStatus` | required, non-empty | Evidence label such as `dataset_match`, `archived_web_capture`, `founder_statement` or `pending_verification`. |
| `privacyTier` | required, non-empty | Privacy classification such as `nickname_level_only`. |
| `civilIdentityLinked` | required, must be `false` | Public profiles must not link nicknames to civil identity. |
| `sensitiveDataIncluded` | required, must be `false` | Public profiles must not include sensitive personal data. |

## Validation

Run:

```bash
python3 scripts/validate_profiles.py
```

The validator checks JSON validity, required fields, non-empty evidence/privacy labels, privacy booleans and `roleName` array shape.

## Archival Boundary

These profiles describe historical nickname-level participation.

They must not expose:

- civil names linked to nicknames;
- private addresses;
- telephone numbers;
- emails;
- IP addresses or full hostmasks;
- private messages;
- sensitive biographical claims;
- individual identity inferred from photographs.

# Nickname Batch 2002-11-28

This batch contains the first structured nickname extraction for Canal Barra.

## Context

- Snapshot/context date: 2002-11-28
- User-provided historical context: day of the Canal Barra 5th anniversary party at Ilha dos Pescadores
- Source family: CanalBarra.com historical cadastro/user list pages
- Male source URL observed in uploaded Wayback text: http://www.canalbarra.com/cadastros/userview2.cfm?sexo=m
- Female list provided by the project founder in the same extraction context

## Counts

| Segment | Rows extracted |
|---|---:|
| Men | 950 |
| Women | 386 |
| Total | 1336 |

The uploaded Wayback text shows the headline `1336 Cadastros!!!`. The extracted men + women lists total exactly 1336 rows, which makes this batch internally consistent as a first archival extraction.

## IRC Status Prefixes

The `@` and `+` symbols are not part of the historical nickname.

They are stored separately in the `irc_status_prefixes` column:

- `@` = operator status marker in the captured listing
- `+` = voice status marker given by operators in the captured listing
- `+@` = combined captured prefix sequence, normalized separately from the display nickname

The cleaned historical identifier is stored as `display_nickname`.

## Historical Rotation Note

This 2002-11-28 batch is a snapshot, not a complete census of every Canal Barra participant across all years.

Some older operator nicknames documented in the June 1999 operators meeting — including JU-RJ, ClaraM and Daiane-de-Ipanema — do not appear in this 2002 list. That absence is historically meaningful: it documents turnover, access-cycle change and migration of some participants to other channels or social spaces.

## Privacy

This batch preserves historical nicknames only. It does not include civil names, emails, IP addresses, full hostmasks, user photos or private messages.

# Nickname Geographic Signals

## Purpose

This folder is reserved for datasets that extract geographic signals from historical Canal Barra nicknames.

The goal is to measure how often the 2002 cadastro list encoded Rio de Janeiro geography inside nicknames, such as Barra, Recreio, Jacarepaguá, Copacabana, Ipanema, Leblon, Tijuca, Méier and other areas.

## Important Boundary

A geographic token inside a nickname is not proof of residence.

Correct interpretation:

```text
nickname_geographic_signal_only
```

Incorrect interpretation:

```text
confirmed_home_address
confirmed_residence
civil_identity_location
```

## Why This Matters

Geographic nicknames help document that Canal Barra was not an abstract chat room. It carried territorial identity.

Examples of useful signals:

```text
Daniel_Recreio -> Recreio dos Bandeirantes signal
[Aviator-RJ-Barra] -> Barra da Tijuca + Rio de Janeiro signal
*_SaRaDo_Do_MeIeR_* -> Méier signal
```

These are cultural and territorial signals, not private-address data.

## Recommended Dataset

Expected file:

```text
data/processed/geography/nickname-geographic-signals-2002.csv
```

Recommended columns:

```text
record_id
snapshot_date
source_capture_date
segment
display_nickname
raw_line
matched_signal
normalized_place
place_type
confidence
inference_scope
residence_claim
notes
```

## Preliminary Extraction Summary

A preliminary extraction from the 1336-row 2002 cadastro dataset produced approximately:

```text
353 geographic signal rows
162 Rio/RJ-level signals
97 Barra da Tijuca signals
33 Recreio dos Bandeirantes signals
13 Jacarepaguá signals
10 Copacabana signals
8 Méier signals
6 Tijuca signals
5 Leblon signals
5 Ilha-area signals
4 Ipanema signals
```

This summary should be regenerated from the final script before being treated as stable.

## Privacy Rule

Do not infer or publish civil location data from nicknames.

The safe claim is:

```text
The nickname list contains explicit geographic self-presentation signals.
```

The unsafe claim is:

```text
These users lived in those neighborhoods.
```

## Core Sentence

**Geographic nicknames are evidence of territorial identity and social self-presentation inside the Canal Barra ecosystem, not evidence of private residence.**
